extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of philosophy/literature (readers of Montaigne)
extracted.subtask_description: Close reading and interpretive analysis of a Renaissance essay (Montaigne) concerned with theology, human reason, and superstition. The page is a literary-philosophical text rather than a formal guideline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid anthropomorphism in speaking of the divine
rubrics_metrics.description: One should not compare or liken the divine nature to human qualities; to do so 'will not blemish and stain it with much imperfection' and is dishonourable to God.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne gives many examples (gods represented eating, clothed, fed, or suffering human passions; deifying heroes; priests prostituting cults) to show how attributing human appetites and needs to gods leads to absurdity and folly. He notes that humans imagine 'themselves in his stead' rather than God.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize the limits of human reason about God
rubrics_metrics.description: Human reason is limited and cannot circumscribe the divine; we must be humble and avoid asserting definitive claims about God's nature based on our finite capacities ('Man cannot be any thing but what he is, nor imagine beyond the reach of his capacity').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne warns against binding God to human laws or logical constraints (e.g., saying 'God cannot do X') and urges reverence in speech: our 'mouths speak it, but our understandings apprehend it not.' Avoid making theological assertions that exceed human comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be skeptical of sensualized promises of the afterlife
rubrics_metrics.description: Promises of paradise that mirror earthly sensual pleasures (tapestry, wine, beautiful women, delicate dishes) are suspect; such accommodations to mortal appetites indicate deception rather than true divine reward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne argues genuine divine recompense should be 'unimaginable, inexplicable, and incomprehensible'—if afterlife pleasures are merely extended versions of earthly sensations, they remain finite and worthless as eternal goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge religious rites and sacrifices by justice and reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Religious practices that cause cruelty (child sacrifice, burning spoils, human immolation, mutilation) are condemnable; religion has historically produced 'most fearful crimes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided: Carthaginian child sacrifice, Lacedemonian whipping of boys, Amestris burying youths alive, priestly abuses. Montaigne treats these as moral and rational grounds to criticize such rites, arguing the will, not outward appearances, should determine culpability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question philosophical arrogance in theological speculation
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophers who presume to define the gods or bind divine action to human concepts (necessity, destiny, mundane causal rules) display arrogance and error.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne cites how schools (Stoics, Plato, Pythagoras) have 'enslaved' God to necessity or given him corporal attributes. He suggests scepticism about sweeping metaphysical claims made with human certitude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doubt simple continuity of personal identity through bodily change (metempsychosis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that a soul preserved through transformations (e.g., phoenix → worm → phoenix) makes the later creature numerically the same person are implausible: 'That which once has ceased to be is no more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne uses biological examples (silkworm → butterfly → worm) to argue that replaced or transformed matter does not preserve personal identity; treat doctrines of transmigration with suspicion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overgeneralizing earthly norms to other worlds
rubrics_metrics.description: If there are many worlds or diverse peoples, one should not assume the principles or rules of our world apply universally; other worlds may have different forms and polities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne points to reports of monstrous or very different peoples and to philosophers (Democritus, Epicurus) who posited many worlds. Use caution when extrapolating terrestrial customs and 'laws of nature' to the cosmos at large.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for the limits and confusions of language in philosophical disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: Many disputes arise from grammatical and linguistic failings; our language is ill-suited to express certain sceptical positions (e.g., Pyrrhonian doubt) and can mislead when used carelessly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne illustrates with paradoxes ('If you say, "I lie," …') and notes that quarrels and wars often spring from contested meanings. He advises acknowledging linguistic limits and speaking reverently about matters beyond clear expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not ascribe ordinary needs or affections to God
rubrics_metrics.description: Assigning to God mundane needs (nourishment, being offended, limited attentions) is a category error—such attributions stem from human projection, not evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montaigne ridicules ideas like gods needing food or being moved by our petty concerns; he urges readers to resist imagining God's operations in human terms (e.g., 'Worldly goods are not goods to God; therefore they are not goods to us').
